reason: Sepals can be setose (bristly). Several examples describe margins or gland borders, but the pair is sound.
Ovaries can be flattened, as in 'ovary flattened globose'. 'hairs flattened' is a different part and should not count.
'Solitary' is a spatial arrangement of the flower. The French examples are correct too.
Pinnae (fern leaf divisions) can be triangular or deltoid.
Pseudostem height in metres is a normal measurement in Musaceae and Zingiberaceae.
A corolla can be silky-hairy (sericeous), usually on the outside.
Orchid pollinia are described as oblong, reniform or ellipsoid.
A corolla tube can be erect or curved. 'Erect basally' is a region qualifier, which is fine.
Staminodes can be short or shorter than the fertile stamens. This is a comparison, but still a valid length quality.
A perigynium (Carex) can have a smooth surface. Some examples are about margins or the beak, which is a minor issue.
A lamina surface can be bristly. The examples mostly refer to margins or teeth, and 'bristlelike' is a shape reading, so check the rule on these.
Seeds can be hemispherical.
A ray flower or ray floret can be glabrous. Some examples are about the rays and rachis of a different part, which is a minor issue.
Fruits such as cypselae can be columnar.
The calyptra of a moss capsule has a shape, such as conic or cylindric. 'Lacerate at the base' is a different quality, but the pair is fine.
A spadix has length × width measurements.
Ray flowers can be hairy (strigose, puberulent, villous). Pilosity is the generic hair attribute.
Boat-shaped glumes (cymbiform) are standard in grasses.
Pedicels and peduncles can be angular in cross-section.
A spadix can be unisexual or bisexual (Araceae).
A calyptra surface can be smooth, scabrous or papillose.
Pedicels and peduncles can be sericeous.
Thorns and spines have width. This is common in cacti.
Seeds can be irregular in shape or outline.
A bract apex can be acute. The apex is the region qualifier, so the pair is sound.
Pyrenes can be grooved, often dorsally.
Bracts have colour, such as straw-coloured.
Seeds can be pear-shaped (pyriform).
The examples ('spur tapering', 'apex tapered') describe other parts, probably a corolla spur or an apex. Short shoots are not described as tapered, so the pair comes from a wrong part reading.
A moss costa can be toothed near the tip.
Sepals can be broadened at the base. 'Midvein broadened' belongs to another part, which is a minor issue.
Presence or absence of paraphyses is a standard character.
A utricle can be glabrous.
Tubers can be tomentose.
A lamina can be flexible or pliable.
Ligulate or liguliform blades are strap-shaped.
Disc florets are bisexual, which PATO calls hermaphrodite.
The examples are about alar cells and auricles (hyaline, reddish), not the leaf. 'Optical quality' is also too generic. Colour or transparency of the alar cells should be used instead.
The abaxial lamina surface can be lanate, with woolly hairs.
Stipules can be spreading or reflexed.
Stipules can be conspicuous or inconspicuous.
A receptacle or receptacle tube can be short.
Pyrene surfaces can be tuberculate, sulcate or smooth. 'Sulcate' is a groove, so some examples map to another quality.
Achenes can be winged. 'Margins winged' is the same reading.
The examples (percurrent, excurrent, 'reaching apex') describe vein course or termination, not position in the PATO sense. They need a dedicated vein-course quality or rule.
The abaxial petal surface has colour.
Pedicels can be velvety (velutinous).
The orchid gynostemium (column) can be erect or curved.
Keels (legume or grass) can be ciliate or ciliolate.
Leaf sheaths can be hispid, including tuberculate-hispid.
A pinnule apex can be acute. The apex is the region qualifier.
Veins and veinlets can be simple (unbranched).
A fern frond can be simple (undivided).
An ovary can be sunken or immersed in the disk or receptacle.
The examples are measurements ('2 mm thick'), so the quality is thickness (PATO_0000915), not 'increased thickness'. A rule should map thickness values to thickness.
Leaf blades can be solid, as opposed to hollow, in grasses, sedges and Juncus.
'Characteristic' is the root PATO term and carries no meaning. The examples are mixed qualities (spreading, stout, slender, toothed), so each should map to its own quality.
Lamina lobes can be rhombic.
'Sinus depth' is a measure of the sinus (the notch), not of the lamina. The bearer should be the sinus, or the quality should be a lobing-depth rule.

The examples ('5 segments', 'of 5 united segments') count the segments of the corona, not corona lobes. A rule would need to say whether 'segments' counts the corona itself or its lobes (see config/flora_counted_parts.tsv).
